sources.label: member email, name, contact details [belongs to a customer; we hold it on their behalf]
sources.note:
Holding data for someone else does not change how sensitive that data is,
so no level moves. It changes who is harmed by its loss and what is owed
when that happens: a processing agreement, deletion on the owner's
instruction, and notification to the owner rather than only to a
regulator. None of that is reachable from a control catalogue keyed on
"we hold data of type X".

It also displaces the jurisdiction question. Regulatory triggers are gated
on the regions of *our* users; for data held on a customer's behalf the
relevant jurisdiction is that customer's, which this profile does not ask
about. Treat any regulatory conclusion as covering our own position only.

sources.label: password hashes, session tokens, recovery codes
sources.note: Theft yields full account takeover and propagates to every other data type. Excluded from the high water mark: FIPS 199 categorises a system by the business information it holds, and credentials are system information present in almost every service. Counting them would put every consumer-facing application on the High baseline, which is a result no team acts on.
